Patagonian mara (Dolichotis patagonum) exhibits a relatively slow life history compared to other caviomorph rodents of similar body size. Neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 650 grams [Wwb = approximately 650 grams], a substantial birth mass characteristic of highly precocial offspring that are fully furred and able to move shortly after delivery. This large investment per offspring is consistent with the species' monogamous mating system and prolonged period of biparental care. Under typical thermoneutral conditions of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the gestation period extends for 85 days [tg = 85 days], which is notably protracted for a rodent and reflects the advanced developmental state of the newborn. This combination of a heavy neonate and a long gestation places the mara at the slow end of the reproductive continuum among South American hystricognaths, a pattern linked to its reliance on stable, predictable food resources in the arid and semi-arid grasslands of its native range.

Sexual maturation in this species is characterized by a marked sexual dimorphism in the timing of puberty. At the physiologically normal body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], female maras attain reproductive maturity at 158 days after birth [tp = 158 days after birth], a pace that allows young females to potentially breed within their first calendar year. Males, by contrast, require a longer developmental period before becoming reproductively viable. At the slightly elevated scrotal temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], which is typical for testicular function in caviomorph rodents, male puberty is reached at 183 days after birth [tp = 183 days after birth]. This divergence in maturation schedules is common among polygynous or monogamous mammals with male-male competition, as the delayed maturity in males may reflect the need for greater body mass and social experience before engaging in successful courtship and territory defense.

Weaning in the Patagonian mara occurs at 65 days after birth [tx = 65 days after birth], a milestone typically reached under the same thermoneutral conditions of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C] that characterize the species' active metabolic period. At this point, the nursing offspring transition from a milk-based diet to solid forage, primarily consisting of grasses and herbs. The weaning age is intermediate among caviomorphs, reflecting a balance between the high nutritional demands of rapid juvenile growth and the constraints imposed by the arid environment where maternal condition can fluctuate seasonally. Juveniles remain closely associated with their parents for several additional months, likely benefiting from vigilance against predators such as the culpeo fox and birds of prey while they continue to refine foraging skills and build body reserves before dispersing from the natal territory.

Adult body size in the Patagonian mara is among the largest of any caviomorph rodent, with individuals reaching a maximum asymptotic mass of approximately 12.5 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 12.5 kilograms]. This substantial size is a key adaptation for cursorial locomotion across the open Patagonian steppe, as a larger body reduces the relative energetic cost of travel and enhances heat retention in the cool, dry climate. The reported range in adult mass extends from 8 up to 16 kilograms, reflecting considerable individual variation influenced by sex, seasonal resource availability, and local habitat quality. Compared to its closest living relatives within the subfamily Dolichotinae, the mara's large size and robust limb morphology represent an evolutionary specialization for fast, sustained running, a trait that allows it to escape predators over open ground rather than seeking refuge in burrows like many other caviids.

Reproduction in the Patagonian mara is characterized by a low annual output typical of a slowly-reproducing, long-lived mammal. Females typically produce 2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 pups per litter], and under favorable conditions they are capable of raising approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of about 4 pups per year. This modest fecundity is a direct consequence of the species' investment in a few, highly precocial young rather than many altricial neonates. Longevity data from captive populations indicate that individuals can survive for up to approximately 14.4 years [am = up to approximately 14.4 years] under standard physiological temperatures of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. This extended lifespan is exceptional among rodents and aligns with the species' slow pace of life, characterized by delayed maturity, low fecundity, and high parental investment in each offspring.
